alphabet.name: a-umlaut
alphabet.sound: eh, as in 'bed' — Bär sounds like 'bair'

alphabet.name: o-umlaut
alphabet.sound: like the 'i' in 'bird', lips rounded — schön

alphabet.name: u-umlaut
alphabet.sound: say 'ee' with rounded lips — für, über

alphabet.name: ie
alphabet.sound: rhymes with 'see' — bier, vier. The opposite of ei.

alphabet.name: ch
alphabet.sound: after a/o/u it's throaty (Bach); after e/i it's soft (ich)

alphabet.name: sp-
alphabet.sound: at the start of a word it's 'shp' — sprechen

alphabet.name: st-
alphabet.sound: at the start of a word it's 'sht' — Straße, Stadt

alphabet.name: r
alphabet.sound: in the throat, and at the end of a word it softens to 'uh'

frameworks.title: der, die, das — and why you can't skip it
frameworks.body: Every German noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das), and the article changes with the sentence's grammar. It is rarely guessable, so learn the article WITH the word — not 'Tisch' but 'der Tisch'. Getting it wrong is understood; getting it right is what makes you sound like you've lived there.

frameworks.title: The verb is second. Always.
frameworks.body: In a main clause the conjugated verb sits in position two, whatever comes first. 'Ich gehe heute ins Kino.' Move 'heute' to the front and the verb still stays second: 'Heute gehe ich ins Kino.' Not 'Heute ich gehe'. This one rule fixes more sentences than any amount of vocabulary.

frameworks.title: …except when it goes right to the end
frameworks.body: After weil, dass, wenn, obwohl, the verb jumps to the end of the clause: 'Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet.' Germans do this without thinking; learners hear the whole sentence before the verb arrives and panic. Expect the wait — it's the single biggest listening hurdle.

frameworks.title: du or Sie
frameworks.body: Sie is the default with strangers, officials, shopkeepers and anyone older you don't know. du is for friends, family, children, and — increasingly — colleagues under about forty. Being offered the du ('Wollen wir uns duzen?') is a small social moment; wait to be offered it rather than assuming.

frameworks.title: Verbs that split in half
frameworks.body: anrufen means 'to call'. But you say 'Ich rufe dich an' — the prefix flies to the end of the sentence. aufstehen, einkaufen, mitkommen and dozens more do this. If a sentence seems to end in a stray little word, that's the other half of the verb catching up.
